subject: Agriculture
title: Qanat Systems
description: A quick, practical guide to Qanat Systems.

hook.text: In ancient Persia, farmers tapped mountain groundwater using tunnels that ran for miles—without any pumps.

buildup.text: A qanat is a gently sloping underground channel that carries water downhill by gravity alone.

discovery.text: Workers dug vertical shafts every 50 meters for access, then connected them with a horizontal tunnel.

twist.text: Because qanats are underground, almost no water evaporates. In a desert, that efficiency is everything.

climax.text: Some qanats built 3,000 years ago still flow today. They're some of the most durable infrastructure ever made.

punchline.text: No pumps, no power, no evaporation—just gravity and genius.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of qanat irrigation systems?
options: Underground channels prevent evaporation and run on gravity alone

details.summary: Qanats are ancient underground water channels that transport groundwater by gravity from highland aquifers to lowland farms. This topic covers their engineering, thousands-of-years history in Persia, and why some qanats still operate in Iran and North Africa today.
details.whyItMatters: Qanats delivered water without pumps or energy for over 3,000 years. They represent a masterclass in sustainable water engineering that modern arid-region agriculture can learn from.
takeaways: Qanats use gravity to transport groundwater through underground tunnels to the surface
Iran still has tens of thousands of qanats, some over 2,500 years old
Qanat systems require no energy input and minimize evaporation losses underground

faq.question: How does a qanat system work?
faq.answer: A qanat taps into a highland water table through a mother well, then channels water underground through a gently sloping tunnel to emerge at the surface in a lowland settlement. Vertical access shafts spaced along the tunnel allow maintenance.

faq.question: Why are qanats considered a sustainable water technology?
faq.answer: Qanats use only gravity—no pumps or fuel—to deliver water. The underground channels minimize evaporation, they draw only the natural flow of aquifers rather than depleting them, and they can operate for centuries with basic maintenance.
